title: Without a campus polling site, Greensboro students marched 45 minutes to vote. Here’s how it came to that
dek: Video of NC A&T and UNCG students walking to Union Square has gone viral on the eve of Election Day. Behind it: a party-line fight over early voting sites that ran from the county board to the state board to federal court.
body:
A video now circulating widely on Instagram and TikTok shows a long column of college students walking along a Greensboro road, set to a caption saying Black students marched 45 minutes just to vote. The footage is real and recent. It comes from this fall’s early voting period in North Carolina, when students at North Carolina A&T State University, the country’s largest historically Black university, along with students from UNC Greensboro and Bennett College, walked together to the nearest early voting site after county and state election officials declined to put one on either campus [1][2][3].

The walk to that site, at Union Square in downtown Greensboro, takes about 45 minutes from A&T [1][2]. How it came to be the closest option is a story about a months-long, mostly party-line dispute over where early voting should happen in a county with two large public universities, and it reached a federal courtroom before a single vote was cast in the midterms [4][5][6].

## The marches

The first march came on Thursday, October 15, the opening day of early voting in North Carolina. More than 100 students from A&T and UNCG set out in heat that reached the mid-80s, according to WFDD. Some stretches of sidewalk were missing or blocked by branches, so parts of the group walked in the street. When they reached Union Square, the line to vote stretched outside the building [1]. Anita Earls, a state Supreme Court justice on this year’s ballot, state Sen. Gladys Robinson and state House Minority Leader Robert Reives, all Democrats, spoke to the students and urged them to bring friends to the polls [1][3].

Student organizer Xavier Jones told WFDD the students would keep showing up “no matter how far you push a polling site off of our campus” [1].

A second, larger march followed on Thursday, October 22. Hundreds of A&T students walked behind the university’s Blue and Gold Marching Machine, joined by Love Island USA winner Trinity Tatum and actress Marsai Martin, both leaders with When We All Vote, the voter-participation group Michelle Obama founded in 2018. Students chanted for their polls to be brought back. Free shuttles took them back to campus afterward [2]. Jimmie Holton, a sophomore who helped organize it, called the long walk in the heat an active barrier to voting [2]. The viral footage appears to come from these October marches; early voting in North Carolina ended Saturday, October 31 [1].

## How the campus sites went away

Both A&T and UNCG hosted early voting sites on campus during the 2024 presidential election. Neither has ever had one in a midterm year, a point the county board has repeatedly made [4][5][6].

The fight began with the March primary. The Guilford County and Jackson County boards, the latter home to Western Carolina University, failed to agree unanimously on early voting plans in late 2025, which sent the decision to the State Board of Elections. The state board, which has a 3-2 Republican majority, adopted plans without campus sites on January 13, 2026, on a party-line vote [3][6]. The College Democrats of North Carolina and four students sued in federal court, arguing the closures targeted young voters in violation of the 26th Amendment and fell hardest on Black students. In February, U.S. District Judge William Osteen denied their request for an emergency order, finding they had not shown standing on the early record, that the burden on students was not severe, and that changing the rules days before voting could confuse voters [6].

For the general election, the Guilford board voted 4-1 on July 21 for a 17-site plan, two more sites than the county used in the 2022 midterm. It kept no sites on the A&T, UNCG or Guilford Technical Community College campuses, but added one at Union Square, an education building shared by students from those schools and Cone Health. Board chair Eugene Lester, a Republican, said Union Square together with the downtown courthouse site would meet students’ needs [4][5]. Carolyn Bunker, a Democrat and the lone no vote, proposed keeping two of the 2024 campus sites and said one in four voters aged 18 to 25 had used those two sites in 2024 [4]. Because the vote was split, it went to the state board, which in August again declined to add an A&T site, also along party lines [3][7].

## The arguments on each side

The county board and the state’s lawyers have argued that Guilford actually expanded early voting compared with the last midterm, that Union Square was chosen precisely because it serves the universities, and that campus sites have historically operated only in presidential years, going back to at least 2002 [4][6]. In court, they also pointed out that students can still register and vote at any early site, request a mail ballot, or vote on Election Day at their assigned precinct [6]. Supporters of the plan statewide have cited limited resources and the number of other voting options [7].

Students and Democrats on the boards answer that most A&T students don’t have cars, that the nearest site is more than a mile away on a route with gaps in the sidewalk and train tracks, and that the campus sites were heavily used when they existed [1][4][7]. At an August hearing, Jeff Carmon, one of the state board’s two Democrats, asked whether anyone could identify “a single voter who is better served by having fewer opportunities to cast a ballot” [3]. Democracy Docket, a voting-rights news site tied to the Democratic lawyer Marc Elias, whose firm represented the students, has called the cuts part of a pattern targeting students [6][7].

Guilford was one of 22 counties this year whose boards split over early voting, the most since 2016, according to WFAE. Most of those disputes concerned weekend and Sunday voting rather than locations [5]. WFAE also reported that county board appointments shifted last year to the state auditor, and that divided votes have risen since [5].

## Why it matters Tuesday

North Carolina is one of the most closely watched states in Tuesday’s election, with an open U.S. Senate seat contested by former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, and Republican Michael Whatley, along with a seat on the state Supreme Court [3]. More than half of the state’s 2022 midterm voters cast ballots early, and nearly three in four did so in 2024 [5].

With early voting over, students who haven’t voted yet will vote on Tuesday at their assigned Election Day precinct, which the State Board of Elections’ voter lookup shows for each registered voter.

Whether the marches change turnout is something the numbers will show only after Tuesday. When We All Vote says events like the October 22 march typically lift turnout by two to four percentage points [2]. Student organizers have said they intend to keep pressing election officials for campus sites in future elections [1].
